rationale: Four military-role cards were reread after narrowing unsupported claims and clarifying the man-at-arms localization. All six current fields have official institutional source passages and explicit interpretation.

cards.editorialAnalysis: Easy is plausible for the familiar role; the prompt scopes documented campaign obligations. Squire, page and man-at-arms describe distinct roles.

fields.claimAnalysis: Royal Armouries documents knights’ obligation to go to war and bring a company of troops.

proofs.title: The Hundred Years’ War 1337–1453 | Royal Armouries
proofs.captureMethod: Complete original institutional HTML/PDF capture was read; the cited passage is transcribed verbatim with locator.
proofs.passage: Knights were a social group below the nobility who were expected to go to war and to bring companies of troops with them. As a result, knights needed to be wealthy enough to buy the sophisticated arms, armour and horses needed for a campaign. Some men received their knighthoods while on campaign: several French soldiers were made knights before the battle of Agincourt. Moreover, Henry V knighted some soldiers at his landing in France and during his march along the Somme for their good service.

fields.claimAnalysis: The squire worksheet supports training and horse/armour care.

proofs.title: Squire Practice | Royal Armouries
proofs.captureMethod: Complete original institutional HTML/PDF capture was read; the cited passage is transcribed verbatim with locator.
proofs.passage:
A squire is someone who is training to become a knight. They need to learn how to use a sword and how to ride a horse.
One of the squire’s most important jobs was to look after their knight’s horse. This meant you would need to feed it, groom it and sweep up all of its poo.
A squire would have to clean lots of armour for their knight.

fields.claimAnalysis: The source adds that some soldiers were knighted during campaigns for service.
